task: Connect the two blue Cat5e network cables from the old phone block to new keystone jacks and join them with a patch cord, then test the link

plan.job_title: Terminate Cat5e cables to keystone jacks
tools_needed: Punch-down tool (a small handle with a blade that pushes wire into a terminal slot and trims the excess — a cheap one costs about $10)
110-type keystone jack x2 (the small snap-in sockets the cable plugs into — buy Cat5e or Cat6, T568B wiring standard)
Wire stripper or a sharp knife
Patch cord (a short pre-made network cable with RJ45 plugs on each end — 1 ft is fine)
Cable tester (a two-piece device that lights LEDs 1–8 to confirm all wires are connected — under $20)

steps.title: Photograph existing punch-down wiring
steps.action: Before touching anything, take a close-up photo of the existing wire colors seated in the old phone block terminals so you have a reference if you need to undo anything.
do_not_touch: yellow-green ground wire at the bottom
any black cables not identified as Cat5e
steps.stop_condition: If any wire or terminal feels warm or looks scorched or melted, stop and contact a professional.
steps.evidence_required: A clear photo showing all wire colors in the punch-down block is saved on your device before you proceed.
highlight_targets: blue Cat5e cables entering the phone/punch-down block
individual wire colors in the terminal slots

steps.title: Unplug or release the first blue Cat5e cable
steps.action: Find the first blue Cat5e cable entering the phone block and gently pull it free from its punch-down slots using the flat-head screwdriver to lever each wire up — do not yank the outer jacket.
do_not_touch: second blue Cat5e cable (leave it in place until its turn)
steps.evidence_required: Photo shows the first blue Cat5e cable hanging free with no wires still seated in the old block terminals.

steps.title: Strip the jacket from the first cable
steps.action: Using the wire stripper or knife, carefully score and remove about 1 inch (25 mm) of the blue outer plastic jacket (called the jacket) from the end of the cable, exposing the four twisted wire pairs inside. Do not nick the individual wire insulation.
do_not_touch: the four twisted pairs themselves — only hold the jacket
steps.evidence_required: Photo shows roughly 1 inch of jacket removed and four twisted pairs visible with no cuts or nicks in the individual wire insulation.
highlight_targets: blue outer jacket to be removed

steps.title: Seat wires into first keystone jack using T568B order
steps.action: Hold the keystone jack (the small snap-in socket) with the T568B color diagram facing you — the color slots are printed on the jack body. Untwist each pair just enough to seat them one by one into the matching color-coded slots: white/orange, orange, white/green, blue, white/blue, green, white/brown, brown.
steps.evidence_required: Photo shows all 8 wires seated in the correct color-coded slots of the jack with none crossed over or missing.
highlight_targets: color-coded slots on the keystone jack body

steps.title: Punch down and trim first keystone jack
steps.action: Press the punch-down tool (blade facing OUTWARD, away from the jack center) firmly onto each wire one at a time — you will hear a click and the tool will trim the excess wire end automatically.
steps.evidence_required: Photo shows all 8 wire ends trimmed flush with the jack — no bare wire sticking up above any slot.
highlight_targets: each wire slot on the jack

steps.title: Repeat steps 2–5 for the second blue Cat5e cable
steps.action: Remove the second blue Cat5e cable from the phone block, strip 1 inch of jacket, seat wires into the second keystone jack in T568B order, and punch them down exactly as you did for the first cable.
steps.evidence_required: Photo shows both keystone jacks completed, all wires punched and trimmed, jacks side by side.

steps.title: Snap jacks into a surface-mount box or coupler
steps.action: Press each keystone jack firmly into a dual surface-mount box (a small plastic housing designed to hold snap-in jacks) or a keystone coupler (a short barrel that joins two jacks face-to-face) until you hear it click — this holds the jacks securely so the patch cord can't wiggle the wires loose.
steps.evidence_required: Photo shows both jacks snapped firmly into the housing or coupler with no gap between jack body and housing edge.
highlight_targets: keystone snap-in slot on the housing or coupler

steps.title: Connect the patch cord between the two jacks
steps.action: Plug one end of the short patch cord (the pre-made cable with RJ45 plastic plugs on each end) into Jack 1 and the other end into Jack 2 — push each plug in until you hear a click.
steps.evidence_required: Photo shows both RJ45 plugs fully seated in their jacks with the locking tab visible and not raised.
highlight_targets: RJ45 plug on each end of the patch cord
port opening of each keystone jack

steps.title: Test the link with a cable tester
steps.action: Unplug the patch cord, plug the cable tester's MAIN unit into Jack 1 and the REMOTE unit into Jack 2, then power the tester on and watch the LEDs numbered 1 through 8 — all 8 LEDs must light in sequence on both units.
steps.stop_condition: If any LED does not light, or if LEDs light in the wrong order (e.g., 1 on main lights against 3 on remote), a wire is mis-seated — unplug the tester, re-open the affected jack, re-seat the wires in the correct color slots, re-punch, and retest.
steps.evidence_required: Photo shows all 8 LEDs lit on both the MAIN and REMOTE units of the cable tester simultaneously.

0.reason: There is no punch-down block visible in this photo — it shows loose wires coming out of a wall hole and what appears to be a router/network device, not a phone block terminal with wires seated in it.
